opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it's one of the biggest missing pieces right now. Today's models are incredibly capable, but they're essentially frozen. You train them, you ship them, and then every interaction starts from zero. If you hire a smart person into your company, on day one they're bright but don't know how your business works. Six months in, they've learned your systems, your customers, the shorthand your team uses, the mistakes not to repeat. That accumulation of context and skill is where most of the value comes from. Models today don't really get that. They're perpetually on day one.

So when we think about deploying these systems inside enterprises, the ability to learn from experience with users is what turns a generic, impressive tool into something that's actually yours, that understands your workflows and gets better the more you use it. Right now we approximate that with retrieval, longer context windows, prompting, and periodic fine-tuning. Those help, but they're patches. They don't give you a model that internalizes feedback the way a person does when they're corrected once and don't make that mistake again.

There's also a bigger-picture reason. We've leaned heavily on scaling pretraining on internet data, and that's giving diminishing returns. The internet is finite, and a lot of the knowledge that matters, how a specific process works or how an expert reasons through an edge case, was never written down. It lives in people's heads and shows up through interaction. If models can learn from that experience, you open up a whole new source of improvement that goes beyond static data.

It's hard, though. You need to do it safely, so the model doesn't learn bad behaviour or leak one customer's information to another. You need it to be efficient, and you need to avoid catastrophic forgetting. But I think whoever cracks learning from experience in a robust way changes how useful these systems are in the real world.

r001.rationale: The response says each interaction starts from zero and models do not internalize user corrections, so corrective effort does not carry forward as lasting learning.

r002.rationale: It explicitly contrasts people who avoid repeating a mistake after one correction with models that do not internalize feedback.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that right now, the way we build these models is deeply strange if you compare it to how anything else in the world gets good at a job. We train a model, we freeze it, and we ship it. And then that model has millions of conversations, makes the same mistakes over and over, and learns absolutely nothing from any of them. The only path for that experience to flow back into the model is through us, the lab, collecting data, filtering it, and running another training cycle months later. That's an incredibly lossy, slow loop.

Contrast that with how a new hire works. You bring someone onto your team, and in their first week they're mediocre at your specific problems. But they watch how you do things, you correct them a few times, they pick up the vocabulary, the edge cases, the things that are obvious to you but written down nowhere. By month three they're genuinely useful, and that's not because they got smarter in some general sense. It's because they accumulated context and corrections from actually doing the work with you.

Today's models are permanently stuck in week one. Every conversation, they show up having forgotten everything. Sure, we bolt on retrieval and long context windows and memory features, and those help, but they're workarounds. The underlying model's behavior doesn't change. It doesn't get better at your codebase or your legal documents or the way your company talks to customers.

For enterprises especially, this is the whole game. The value isn't in a model that's brilliant at trivia. It's in a model that knows the hundred idiosyncratic things about how your organization operates, and that knowledge lives in the interactions, not in any dataset we can scrape. So if you want a system that actually compounds in value over time rather than being a static tool, learning from experience with the user isn't a nice-to-have. It's the mechanism by which the thing becomes yours.

And I'd add, it also changes the economics of intelligence. If every improvement has to come from the frontier lab running a bigger pretraining run, progress is gated on a handful of companies and enormous compute. If models can improve through use, then the gains get distributed. Every deployment becomes a source of improvement. I think that's a much healthier trajectory for the field, and frankly a much more realistic path to models that are genuinely reliable in the messy, specific environments where people actually need them.

r001.rationale: It says models forget everything between conversations and learn nothing from their repeated interactions, while contrasting that with accumulating user corrections.

r002.rationale: It says models make the same mistakes repeatedly and explains that learning from corrections would let them improve through experience with the user.

astra-6.text:
Because right now, there’s this strange disconnect: you can teach a model something in a conversation, and it can use that information, but that doesn’t necessarily carry over to the next time you interact with it. You’re effectively starting over. If you had a colleague who forgot everything you’d taught them at the end of every day, there would be a pretty hard ceiling on how useful they could be.

Learning from experience lets a model get better at working with you. It can understand your preferences, learn the context of your work, and improve when you tell it, “That wasn’t what I meant—here’s what I actually needed.” A lot of that information isn’t sitting on the public internet. It emerges through doing things together.

The important distinction is between producing a plausible answer and learning what actually works. When a model can take feedback from an interaction and use it to do better next time, you have something that can keep improving through use. That’s a really powerful capability.

r001.rationale: The response says information taught in one conversation may not carry over to the next, leaving the user effectively starting over.

r002.rationale: It says a model can use feedback about what the user actually needed to do better next time, communicating that it can avoid repeating corrected mistakes.

sol-6.1.text:
Because right now, there’s this strange disconnect: you can teach a model something in a conversation, and it can use that information, but then the conversation ends and that learning is gone. The next time you interact with it, you’re starting over.

If you want AI to be a useful collaborator, it needs to learn from working with you. What are you trying to accomplish? What does a good result look like to you? When you correct it, can it use that correction to do better next time? Otherwise, you’re continually spending effort explaining the same things.

And a lot of what makes someone good at a job comes from experience, rather than something you can read in a document. You try something, get feedback, and adjust. Giving models that ability would let them become more useful through actually doing the work. The important challenge is making sure they learn the right things, and that users have control over what they remember.

r001.rationale: It says learning from a conversation is gone when it ends, so the next interaction starts over and the user must explain the same things again.

r002.rationale: It asks whether the model can use a correction to do better next time and says otherwise the user keeps explaining the same things, conveying that it can avoid repeating corrected mistakes.
